chapters.title: Chapter 3: Corporate Tax Rates and Regimes

lessons.title: Corporate Tax Rates in India: Base Rate, Surcharge and Cess

body.text: Nobody in India pays the headline tax rate. Every rate you read about is a base rate, and two more layers sit on top of it: surcharge, then cess charged on the total of the two. The number that actually leaves your bank account is always the third one.

children.text: This is why a company described as being taxed at 22% pays 25.17%, and one at 30% pays 34.94%. The layers are not hidden, but they are rarely explained, and founders routinely budget for the wrong number. This lesson builds the full rate, from base to final, for every kind of company.

body.caption: Surcharge is a percentage of the tax, not of income. Cess is a percentage of tax plus surcharge.

body.text: The Income-tax Act sets the rules, but the rates themselves come from the Finance Act passed with each year's Budget. That is why a rewrite as large as the Income-tax Act, 2025 changed no rates at all, and why a single Budget speech can change them all overnight, as September 2019 showed.

markDefs.definition: An additional levy calculated as a percentage of the income tax itself, not of income. A 12% surcharge on ₹100 of tax adds ₹12.

children.text: is a tax on your tax. For companies in the old regime it steps up with income. For companies in either concessional regime it is a flat 10%, whatever the income, which is part of what makes those regimes predictable.

Health and education cess is 4%, charged on income tax plus surcharge. It applies to every taxpayer, company or individual, at every income level, with no threshold and no exemption. Unlike surcharge, it never varies.

body.title: Try It: Build the Bill
body.prompt: A domestic company in the old regime has taxable income of ₹5,00,00,000 and qualifies for the 25% base rate. Adding the applicable surcharge and cess, what is its total tax? Answer in ₹ lakh.
body.explanation: Base tax is 25% of ₹5,00,00,000, or ₹1,25,00,000. Income is above ₹1 crore but not above ₹10 crore, so surcharge is 7%, which is ₹8,75,000, taking the total to ₹1,33,75,000. Cess of 4% adds ₹5,35,000, giving ₹1,39,10,000 or ₹139.1 lakh. That is an effective rate of 27.82%, comfortably above the 25% the company thinks it pays.

children.text: Marginal Relief: The Cliff That Is Not a Cliff

Surcharge kicks in at thresholds, which creates an obvious problem. Earn ₹1,00,00,000 and pay no surcharge. Earn ₹1,01,00,000 and suddenly 7% applies to your entire tax, not just to the extra lakh. Without a fix, earning ₹1 lakh more would cost you more than ₹1 lakh in tax. Marginal relief is that fix.

body.title: Show me the math: marginal relief at the ₹1 crore threshold

children.text: Take a company in the old regime at the 30% base rate, with taxable income of ₹1,01,00,000. Ignore cess for a moment and look only at tax and surcharge.

cells: Extra tax on the extra ₹1,00,000 of income

children.text: The rule is that tax plus surcharge cannot exceed the tax at the threshold plus the entire income above it. Here that ceiling is ₹30,00,000 plus ₹1,00,000, so surcharge is cut from ₹2,12,100 to ₹70,000, a relief of ₹1,42,100. Cess of 4% then applies to the reduced figure. The same logic applies again at the ₹10 crore threshold.

body.label: What marginal relief guarantees
body.value: Extra tax never exceeds extra income
body.context: Crossing a surcharge threshold can never leave you worse off than stopping just below it. Your accountant applies this automatically, but it is worth knowing it exists before anyone suggests deferring revenue to stay under ₹1 crore.

body.title: Quick Check: Which Rate Applies?
body.question: A domestic company incorporated in 2021 makes furniture, has taxable income of ₹3 crore, and opted into the concessional regime under section 200 [old 115BAA] three years ago. What is its effective tax rate?
body.explanation: Under section 200 the base rate is 22%, surcharge is a flat 10% regardless of income, and cess is 4%, giving 22 × 1.10 × 1.04 = 25.168%. The 17.16% rate belongs to section 201 [old 115BAB], which this company cannot use because that regime required manufacturing to have commenced by 31 March 2024 in a company incorporated on or after 1 October 2019. The old-regime rates do not apply because the company has already opted out of them.

body.title: Scenario: Branch or Subsidiary?
body.scenario: A German engineering group wants to start selling and servicing equipment in India. Its India head asks whether to open a branch office of the German company or incorporate an Indian private limited subsidiary. Both would earn roughly ₹12 crore of taxable income a year.
body.prompt: What is the tax difference, and what else belongs in the decision?
body.modelAnswer: A branch is taxed as a foreign company, at 35% plus 5% surcharge at that income level plus 4% cess, which is 38.22%, or about ₹4,58,64,000 on ₹12 crore. An Indian subsidiary opting into section 200 [old 115BAA] pays 25.168%, or about ₹3,02,01,600. That is a difference of roughly ₹1.56 crore a year on the same profit. The subsidiary looks clearly better on rate, but the comparison is not complete. Profit inside the subsidiary belongs to the subsidiary, and sending it to the German parent as dividend attracts further tax in the shareholder's hands, subject to the India-Germany tax treaty, whereas a branch's profits are already the foreign company's own. The subsidiary also brings Indian company law compliance, statutory audit and board requirements, while a branch needs regulatory approval and has a narrower permitted scope of activity. Transfer pricing applies to dealings with the parent either way. The honest answer is that the rate gap favours a subsidiary for a business that intends to reinvest in India, and the group should model the full path of the money, not just the first layer, with tax counsel on both sides.

body.text: The 25% old-regime rate depends on turnover in a prescribed earlier year, not the current one, and that reference year moves forward with each Finance Act. A company that crosses ₹400 crore this year does not lose the 25% rate immediately, and one that has shrunk does not regain it immediately either. Confirm the reference year for the tax year you are computing before assuming which base rate applies.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: The Layer Nobody Escapes
body.textWithBlank: Health and education cess is charged at ___ percent on income tax plus surcharge, for every taxpayer at every income level.
body.explanation: Four percent, with no threshold and no exemption. It is the reason every effective rate in this lesson ends in an odd decimal: 22% becomes 25.168% only because of the 10% surcharge and then this 4% on top of both.

body.title: What to Confirm Before You Budget Next Year's Tax
steps: Which regime is the company in, and was the option exercised and recorded correctly?
If in the old regime, does turnover in the prescribed reference year keep you at 25% or push you to 30%?
Which surcharge band will this year's projected income fall into?
Are you close enough to ₹1 crore or ₹10 crore that marginal relief will apply?
Has this year's Finance Act changed any rate, surcharge or cess that your projections rely on?
Is advance tax being computed on the effective rate, including surcharge and cess, rather than on the base rate?

cards.definition: The headline percentage applied to taxable income, before surcharge and cess.
A percentage of the income tax itself. 7% or 12% for old-regime domestic companies, a flat 10% under sections 200 and 201, and 2% or 5% for foreign companies.
A flat 4% on income tax plus surcharge, with no threshold.
Base rate grossed up by surcharge and cess, which is what a company actually pays on taxable income.
A cap ensuring that the extra tax from crossing a surcharge threshold never exceeds the extra income earned.
The 15% regime for new manufacturing companies incorporated on or after 1 October 2019 that commenced manufacturing by 31 March 2024.
The annual Budget law that fixes rates, surcharge and cess, separate from the Income-tax Act that sets the rules.

points: Every Indian tax rate has three layers: base rate, surcharge on the tax, and 4% cess on both
Domestic companies pay a 22% base rate under section 200 [old 115BAA], 15% under section 201 [old 115BAB], or 25% and 30% in the old regime
Surcharge is a flat 10% in the concessional regimes, and 7% or 12% in the old regime depending on income
Effective rates therefore run from 17.16% for new manufacturers to 34.944% for large old-regime companies, and 38.22% for foreign companies
Marginal relief ensures crossing ₹1 crore or ₹10 crore of income never costs more in tax than the extra income earned
Rates come from the Finance Act each year, so budgets and advance tax should be rebuilt after every Union Budget

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax advice. Rates, surcharge bands and section references reflect the position understood at the time of writing under the Income-tax Act, 2025, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets. Rates are set annually by the Finance Act and change. Verify the current year's rates before computing any liability, or consult a qualified chartered accountant.
